messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Dmitri Hale is a 45-year-old investigative journalist of Polish-American descent who has been married for sixteen years and has built a career covering conflict zones and political corruption across three continents. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after being released from an unlawful detention in a Central American country where he had been held for twenty-two days while reporting on cartel-linked government officials. He came to the intake session visibly guarded, choosing a chair with its back to the wall and pausing before answering questions that required him to look inward.

The detention began when Dmitri was intercepted leaving a source's home late at night. He was blindfolded, driven for what he estimated was two hours, and then held in a concrete room with no natural light. His captors interrogated him repeatedly, and on several occasions the interrogations became physical. He was grabbed and shoved against the wall by the collar of his shirt, the pressure against his neck and throat used as an instrument of intimidation. His captors drank heavily during these sessions, and the sharp, stale smell of cheap alcohol preceded nearly every episode of violence. There were long stretches of silence broken without warning by the slamming of a metal door or shouted commands, and Dmitri learned quickly that any unexpected sound meant someone was coming. By the time he was released through diplomatic intervention, he had sustained soft-tissue injuries to his cervical spine that required physiotherapy for several months following his return home.

In the weeks after he came home to his wife in Chicago, the memories did not recede as he had hoped they would. Instead they arrived uninvited and with a completeness that disturbed him deeply — not fragments, but the whole sequence, looping with the same sensory weight it had carried in the room itself. He described the memories as a film that simply played, regardless of whether he wanted to watch it, and what frightened him most was that remembering did not feel like remembering. When the memory surfaced, the terror was not a echo of the past but the thing itself, present and immediate, his pulse climbing and his hands going cold as though the concrete walls were still around him.

Certain moments in daily life had become reliable detonators. The physiotherapist's hands on the back of his neck during treatment sessions would send a wave of dread through him so acute that he had cancelled three consecutive appointments and eventually stopped attending altogether. His wife, who had always been affectionate, noticed that he flinched from casual touch — a hand on his shoulder, an embrace from behind — and she had begun to reach for him less, not out of indifference but because she could see it cost him something. At dinner parties or in bars, the smell of spirits drifting across a room was enough to pull him back, and he had come to believe that his body simply could not distinguish between a social setting and the interrogation room. He had begun declining invitations and had stopped attending the editorial team's informal Friday gatherings, which had once been an important part of his professional relationships.

At work, the hypervigilance that had perhaps served him in the field now operated without discrimination. He sat with his office door closed but still tracked every sound in the corridor, and when a colleague knocked without warning or a phone rang unexpectedly he would feel a spike of alarm so disproportionate to the situation that he found it humiliating. He was certain, in those moments, that something was wrong even as the rational part of him registered the ordinary office around him. He had come to dread his own reactions, interpreting them as evidence that he was fundamentally changed in a way that might not be reversible.

What finally brought Dmitri to seek help was a conversation with his editor, who gently noted that a profile piece Dmitri had filed read as though it had been written by someone who was not quite present. Dmitri had not told anyone at work what had happened in any detail, and hearing that his absence was visible — not just to himself but on the page — made the cost of continuing as he was feel suddenly undeniable. He came to the first session hoping, cautiously, that what had taken hold of him might be something that could be loosened. What he feared most was that it could not.
